title: Multiplexing, spread spectrum and switching
subtitle: How many conversations share one wire, and how a call finds its way across a network.

sections.title: Frequency-division and time-division multiplexing
sections.body: Multiplexing combines many signals onto one medium. FDM gives each signal its own frequency band (radio stations, cable TV) with guard bands between them. TDM gives each signal the whole channel for a short time slot in rotation: synchronous TDM wastes slots when a source is idle; statistical TDM allocates slots on demand. WDM is FDM for light: each colour carries a channel on one fibre.

worked.why: A T1 line multiplexes 24 voice channels, each 64 kb/s, plus 8 kb/s framing.

questions.prompt: Why does FDM need guard bands?

choices.text: To keep neighbouring signals from interfering as filters are not perfectly sharp.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each band is separated by unused spectrum.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — time-division multiplexing
figures.note: Three sources take turns in fixed time slots.

sections.title: ADSL and xDSL
sections.body: ADSL uses the copper pair in three frequency bands: voice (0–4 kHz), upstream and a much wider downstream band — asymmetric because home users download more than they upload. It uses discrete multitone: the band is split into 4 kHz sub-channels, each modulated with as many bits as its own signal-to-noise ratio allows. Speed falls with distance from the exchange.

questions.prompt: What does the “A” in ADSL stand for?

choices.text: Asymmetric — downstream is faster than upstream.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Most traffic flows toward the user.

sections.title: Spread spectrum and CDMA
sections.body: Spread spectrum deliberately uses far more bandwidth than needed: FHSS hops the carrier among frequencies in a pseudo-random sequence; DSSS multiplies each bit by a fast chipping code. In CDMA every user has a different orthogonal code and all transmit at once on the same band; the receiver recovers one user by correlating with that user’s code — the others average to zero.

worked.why: Two users with orthogonal codes c₁ = (+1 +1 +1 +1) and c₂ = (+1 −1 +1 −1). User 1 sends bit +1, user 2 sends bit −1.
The channel carries the sum: c₁ − c₂ = (0, 2, 0, 2).
Receiver for user 1 correlates with c₁ and divides by 4.

questions.prompt: In CDMA how does a receiver pick out one user from the combined signal?

choices.text: By listening on a special frequency.
By correlating with that user’s spreading code.
By waiting for its time slot.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Orthogonal codes make other users cancel.

sections.title: Circuit, message and packet switching
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a path for the whole call (telephone): guaranteed rate, set-up delay, idle capacity wasted. Message switching stores and forwards whole messages. Packet switching cuts data into packets routed separately: efficient for bursty traffic, variable delay. Two flavours: datagram (each packet routed independently, may arrive out of order) and virtual circuit (a path is set up first; packets follow it in order).

worked.why: Send a 1.5 MB file over 4 hops of 1 Mb/s each, propagation ignored. Packet size 1500 B, 1000 packets.
Store-and-forward message switching: each hop retransmits the whole file: 4 × 12 s = 48 s.
Packet switching pipelines: first hop takes 12 s, then the last packet needs 3 more hop-times of 12 ms: ≈ 12.04 s.

questions.prompt: Why is packet switching better for bursty data?

choices.text: Capacity is shared; nothing is reserved during silences.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Circuit switching wastes the idle reserved path.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — a circuit-switched call
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Sender] as s
[Switch A] as a
[Switch B] as b
[Receiver] as r
s -> a : call setup
a -> b : setup
b -> r : setup
r --> s : connected
s -> r : data over the reserved path
s -> r : teardown");

sections.title: Switching devices
sections.body: A crossbar switch connects any input to any output with n² crosspoints; multistage (Banyan/Clos) networks use fewer small switches at the price of possible blocking. A packet switch adds buffers to hold packets contending for the same output.

questions.prompt: Crosspoints in an n × n crossbar?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One crosspoint for every input–output pair.

problems.prompt: A 16 × 16 crossbar has how many crosspoints, and an omega network with 2×2 switches how many switches?

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• FDM splits frequency, TDM splits time, WDM splits colour, CDMA splits by code.
  • Circuit switching reserves; packet switching shares.
